title: Platform Governance, Portability & Dependency Atlas
purpose: Study online platforms as governance and dependency systems: who sets rules, how visibility and moderation operate, what users can carry elsewhere, and where creators or communities become structurally dependent.

questions: Object removal, reach reduction, account restriction, demonetization, age/geographic gating or other measures?
Can a user challenge a decision?
Is there a reason code, evidence, timeline and independent review?
Which distribution systems matter: following, search, recommendation, trending, notifications?
Which criteria are known, inferred or opaque?
Who controls payouts, advertising eligibility, subscriptions, donations, commerce or sponsorship tools?
Can users retrieve content, metadata, contact graph, subscribers/followers, account history or moderation history?
Can identity, audience, content or social graph move across services?
Which courts, regulators, auditors, researchers or public reporting systems can inspect the platform?

dependency_vector.measure: share of reachable audience concentrated on one platform
share of creator/community income dependent on one platform
degree to which reputation/account identity cannot be moved
degree to which history/content disappears if the service closes or access is lost
share of discovery controlled by platform-owned ranking
dependence on platform-specific production, community or moderation tools
ability to export/reconstruct follower, subscription or community relationships
ability to participate or publish across multiple platforms without prohibitive cost

resilience_patterns: portable archives preserve memory even when reach is lost
open protocols can reduce identity/audience lock-in but do not automatically solve moderation or abuse
creator-owned mailing lists/domains/archives can preserve direct reach
platform dependence can be high even when formal exit is technically easy
boundary_rules: Removal or reduced reach is not automatically censorship in the legal sense; jurisdiction and actor matter.
Opaque ranking does not prove intentional suppression of a particular person or viewpoint.
High engagement does not prove algorithmic favoritism without stronger evidence.
Platform migration can change governance, incentives and community composition at the same time.
